title: A Poincare section and limit cycle: is the motion periodic or chaotic?
summary: A long trajectory is reduced to the points where it pierces a chosen plane in one direction. A periodic orbit leaves a few repeating points; a chaotic one leaves a scattered set that traces out a thin curve or fractal.

media.alt: Top row: two trajectories in the x-y plane, a double loop on the left (periodic) and a dense spiral band on the right (chaotic), each crossed by an orange dashed horizontal line with pink dots on it. Bottom row: pink points of the section: two isolated dots on the left, a long thin curve of dots on the right.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Is the motion periodic or chaotic?
read_the_figure.axes: Top: x and y of the trajectory, equal scale; the amber dashed line is the section plane y = 0. Pink dots: crossings with dy/dt > 0 and x > 0. Bottom: the section itself, (x at crossing, z at crossing). Left column: parameter c = 3. Right: c = 5.7. The caption states the section plane.
look_at: How many distinct crossing points does the left orbit leave and how many does the right?
How many loops does the left orbit make before closing?
Where do the right-hand points lie: scattered anywhere or on a curve?
What does the label on the left bottom panel say, and does it match the dots?
as_drawn: The system is x' = -y - z, y' = x + 0.2y, z' = 0.2 + z(x - c), with c = 3 and c = 5.7. The first quarter of each run (the transient) is discarded; 52 section points are drawn for each case.

For c = 3 the 52 points sit at only two distinct places, (4.85, 0.99) and (5.70, 2.65), and the orbit has two loops: a period-2 cycle. The label 'one fixed point' on the figure is wrong; two points are visible.
For c = 5.7 all 52 points are distinct and lie on a thin curve between x = 3.6 and 9.8; the label 'fractal band' fits.
read_the_figure.proves: That, for the chosen section and parameter, the return points repeat (periodic) or do not (aperiodic, on a thin curve). It does not prove chaos by itself: a quasi-periodic orbit or one with a very long period can look similar.
if_wrong: Section plane not stated: the points cannot be reproduced.
Crossings from both directions counted: each loop is counted twice.
Transient not removed: stray points from the approach to the attractor look like extra structure.

terms.meaning: A surface in state space; one records each point where the trajectory crosses it in a chosen direction.
The map from one crossing to the next, P from the section to itself.
A closed trajectory; it leaves finitely many section points (period n: n points).
An isolated periodic orbit that nearby trajectories approach.
Bounded, aperiodic motion with sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
A section point mapped to itself: a period-1 orbit.

remember: Period-n orbit = n distinct section points, repeating.
Aperiodic: points never repeat, and they fill a curve or fractal set.
State the section plane and the crossing direction.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The top row shows the trajectory as a line and the section as a dashed line with the crossing points. The bottom row shows only the points, in the section's own coordinates (x, z). Colour separates the cases; the number of distinct points is the result.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A continuous trajectory is hard to compare, but its crossings of a plane form a discrete sequence, the return map. If the orbit is periodic the sequence repeats: a few points. If not, it never repeats and a picture of the points reveals the geometry of the attractor in one lower dimension. The reduction trades a 3D curve for a 2D set of dots, which is much easier to read.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A short run gives few points and little structure. Counting both crossing directions double-counts. A long transient adds stray points. The section choice matters: a plane tangent to the flow gives nonsense. And chaos in a picture is circumstantial: it is the sensitivity to initial conditions that defines it, which no static plot shows.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The stated section plane lets anyone reproduce the points; a different plane gives a different set of dots. This render states it in the caption and draws it as the amber dashed line, which is the only item on the list, so the rest of the reading rests on counting dots honestly, as the as-drawn note shows.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: To see parameter dependence, plot the section coordinate against the parameter (a bifurcation diagram). To test chaos, estimate the largest Lyapunov exponent or plot the first-return map x(k+1) against x(k). A power spectrum separates periodic (lines) from chaotic (broadband). A time series shows the raw signal.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the first-return map x(k+1) against x(k) for each case with the diagonal: for c = 3 two points pair up off the diagonal, for c = 5.7 the dots form a curve.

steps.title: The return map and periodic orbits
steps.note: For c = 3 the numerical crossings alternate between (4.848, 0.993) and (5.705, 2.654): P maps each to the other, so P squared fixes both and the orbit is period 2 (two loops).

steps.title: Stability of a periodic orbit
steps.note: A stable cycle attracts nearby orbits, so the section points collapse onto the same two dots; in the chaotic case nearby orbits separate and the 52 points are all different (52 distinct values at three decimals).

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) how many distinct section points on the left and on the right? (2) What is the period on the left? (3) Why does the left label disagree with the dots?

solution.text: Left: two distinct places, near (4.85, 1.0) and (5.70, 2.65); right: 52 different points.
Two loops in the x-y plot and two section points: period 2.
The label says one fixed point, but one fixed point would mean a single dot and a single-loop orbit. The picture shows two dots and two loops, so the label is wrong.

worked.answer: Left: two points, a period-2 orbit (the figure's 'one fixed point' text is wrong); right: 52 distinct points along a thin curve, consistent with chaos.

analyze.q: Why discard the first part of the trajectory?
If the left orbit were period 1, what would the section show?
A student counts crossings in both directions. How does the section change and what error follows?

evaluate.q: A paper says 'the section shows a fractal band, hence chaos'. What additional evidence would you ask for?
evaluate.hint: Lyapunov exponent, return map, sensitivity test.

create: Plot the first-return map x(k+1) against x(k) for both cases with the diagonal.
Make a bifurcation diagram: x at the section against c from 2 to 6 and mark c = 3 and c = 5.7.

checks.q: What does a periodic orbit of period 3 leave on a Poincare section?
checks.answer: Three distinct points visited in a repeating cycle.

checks.q: Why must you state the section plane and crossing direction?
checks.answer: A different plane or direction gives a different set of points, so the result cannot be reproduced or compared otherwise.

checks.q: A section shows 500 points on a smooth closed curve. Is the motion necessarily chaotic?
checks.answer: No: quasi-periodic motion on a torus also fills a closed curve in the section; chaos needs sensitivity to initial conditions and a thin or fractal set.
